article.overview: A thermal volatile analyser is an instrument class that heats a sample of lunar soil or rock in a controlled sequence and identifies the gases and vapours released at each temperature step, usually with a mass spectrometer. Water and other volatile compounds are held in regolith and ice with different strengths and are released at different temperatures, so a heating sequence can show which volatile species a sample contains and give an indication of how much is present [1][2]. "Thermal volatile analyser" is a catalogue class name rather than the name of one lunar instrument, and no flown lunar instrument carrying exactly this name was identified in this review. This article therefore covers related evolved-gas instruments, lunar concepts, a prototype and flown hardware, and assesses the status of each separately. No verified direct image asset was retrieved, so the article contains no embedded images.
article.description: A thermal volatile analyser places a sample of known mass in an oven or analysis cell, raises the oven temperature along a programmed ramp, and passes the released gas to an analytical detector. The detector is commonly a mass spectrometer, which identifies each gas from its mass-to-charge ratio. Because each volatile leaves the sample within a characteristic temperature range, the temperature at which a gas appears gives information about how it was held in the sample, not only what it is. Designs differ in their detectors. The Phoenix TEGA instrument paired its ovens with a magnetic-sector mass spectrometer [3], the VAPoR concept proposed a miniature pyrolysis mass spectrometer derived from the SAM instrument suite [4], and the Chang'e-7 LUWA concept combines a tunable laser spectrometer with a time-of-flight mass spectrometer [1][2]. On the Moon, the central problem is that the volatiles of greatest interest, particularly water ice in permanently shadowed regions, may be present at low concentrations and must be sampled, heated and measured without contamination or loss. A thermal volatile analyser is therefore usually one link in a chain that includes sample acquisition (a drill, a scoop or an astronaut-collected sample), transfer to the oven, heating, gas analysis and data processing [1][2][4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose is to determine the volatile content of lunar material: which volatile species are present and roughly in what amount. Water is the central target. The LightWAVE paper argues that water in icy regolith in permanently shadowed regions is a key in-situ resource, that no planned mission would quantify its abundance, and that Apollo samples are unsuitable for this purpose because they may have lost volatiles and were not collected from shadowed regions [1]. The VAPoR concept lists three measurement objectives: isotope ratios of carbon-, hydrogen-, oxygen- and nitrogen-containing volatiles, including water, to establish their origin; the processes that disperse or destroy terrestrial organic compounds on the lunar surface; and the abundance of volatiles that can be released from regolith for in-situ resource utilisation (ISRU) technology development [4]. The LUWA paper states its goal as the first in-situ detection of water ice and volatiles at the lunar south pole, and expects its data to clarify the abundance, origin and distribution of lunar water [2]. Its ground-test isotope result, a delta-D precision of ±50‰, is reported in the abstract [2]. The scientific interpretation of such isotope ratios is outside the scope of the sources consulted and is not asserted here.
article.operating_principle: Evolved-gas analysis, the basic principle of this instrument class, has four stages. First, a sample of known mass is loaded into an oven or analysis cell. Second, the oven is heated along a controlled temperature ramp. Third, the released gases are transferred to the analyser, sometimes after cleaning. Fourth, the analyser identifies and quantifies the gases as a function of temperature. The temperature range differs between designs. The TEGA ovens were heated to about 1000 °C [3]. The VAPoR concept cites vacuum pyrolysis at temperatures up to 1400 °C as an efficient way to release volatiles from lunar regolith, and its breadboard heated a lunar regolith simulant to 1200 °C under vacuum [4]. The VAPoR design uses a six-cup carousel and a gas handling system with no pumps or carrier gases; a calcium oxide scrubber removes CO2 and CO from the gas stream, and a separate chemical getter removes active gases, which are regenerated by heating to 900 °C [4]. The LUWA abstract does not give heating temperatures [2]. Two analytical approaches appear in the sources. In the LightWAVE concept, a modified commercial residual gas analyser (a quadrupole mass spectrometer) identifies species by mass-to-charge ratio, and water is quantified by combining the water partial pressure with the ideal gas law [1]. In the LUWA concept, a tunable laser spectrometer measures H2O and HDO, a time-of-flight mass spectrometer analyses gases below 200 atomic mass units, and a differential absorption spectrometer on a probe leg pre-detects water ice during drilling [2]. The two approaches are not equivalent, and their performance cannot be compared directly from the sources consulted.
article.scientific_importance: Remote sensing has found water ice at the Moon's poles, but it cannot directly establish whether water exists in permanently shadowed regions or where it came from [2]. Lunar Prospector detected high concentrations of hydrogen at the poles, which may indicate water or other volatiles in the regolith, but hydrogen alone does not establish the form or origin of the material [4]. In-situ heating and gas analysis are therefore proposed to complement orbital data. Laboratory studies of Apollo soils show that heating them under vacuum releases gases including H2, N2, CO2, CO, SO2, O2 and several noble gases [4], which indicates the kind of measurement an in-situ instrument would need to make. The approach also has flight heritage in planetary exploration. The Phoenix Thermal and Evolved-Gas Analyzer, flown on Mars, used a heating sequence and mass spectrometry to examine soil and rock samples [3]. Its heritage is relevant to lunar work, but the Mars environment and sample chemistry differ, and TEGA results do not establish lunar volatile content.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a thermal volatile analyser. Designs range from a single-use oven with a mass spectrometer to multi-channel systems that combine a laser spectrometer, a time-of-flight analyser and a probe-mounted absorption spectrometer. The values below describe specific historical, flown, prototype, planned or proposed examples. Where a value is not stated in the consulted source, it is recorded as not publicly specified, and no value has been estimated.

examples.name: Thermal and Evolved-Gas Analyzer (TEGA), Phoenix Mars lander
examples.type: Flown instrument on Mars (not a lunar instrument)
examples.overall_dimensions: not publicly specified in the consulted source
examples.heating_or_sampling: Eight single-use thermal analyser cells, each with its own oven and sample-receiving funnel; about 50 mg of fine-grained soil or rock fragments heated from ambient to about 1000 °C.
examples.oven_dimensions: about 2.4 mm diameter and 8 mm long
examples.gas_analysis: Magnetic-sector mass spectrometer; stated detection limit 10 parts per billion.
examples.calorimetry: Each cell collects calorimetric data from the power applied to the oven during the programmed ramp.
examples.notes: Included as the best-documented flown example of the thermal evolved-gas approach. Mass, dimensions and power are not stated in the consulted source.

examples.name: LightWAVE (Light Water Analysis and Volatile Extract)
examples.status: Development concept under calibration; no measured results reported in the consulted paper
examples.overall_dimensions: not publicly specified in the consulted source
examples.heating_or_sampling: Heats icy lunar regolith on the surface; heating temperatures not stated.
examples.gas_analysis: Modified commercial off-the-shelf residual gas analyser (quadrupole mass spectrometer). Water quantitation from water partial pressure and the ideal gas law.
examples.calibration: Calibration constants and procedures not stated.
examples.notes: Paper presents methodology only. No measured values, mass, power, dimensions or flight status are given.

examples.name: Volatile Analysis by Pyrolysis of Regolith (VAPoR)
examples.type: Pyrolysis mass spectrometer concept with laboratory breadboard
examples.status: Concept study selected for funding in 2007 under NASA Lunar Sortie Science Opportunities; laboratory breadboard built; no flown instrument reported

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No single set of dimensions applies to the class. The TEGA ovens were about 2.4 mm in diameter and 8 mm long, and the VAPoR concept estimated an instrument volume of about 20 x 43 x 51 cm. The LUWA and LightWAVE dimensions are not publicly specified in the consulted sources. Dimensions should be tied to a named instrument and source.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Stated values are limited to the examples above. The VAPoR concept estimated 7 to 15 kg, the Lunar Volatiles Scout analyser is stated as under 500 g, and the Lunar Volatiles Scout sampler and analyser together are stated as under 1.5 kg. TEGA, LightWAVE, LUWA and PRIME-1 values are not publicly specified in the consulted sources.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The VAPoR concept estimated 18 W average and 36 W peak. Other examples do not state power in the consulted sources. Heating power depends on oven design and temperature ramp, and no value is asserted for the other examples.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar volatile analyser must operate in vacuum, through extreme surface temperature swings, radiation and dust. Its sample path must avoid contamination from the lander, the drill or the atmosphere, because the gases of interest may be present at very low concentrations [2][6]. Thermal control is needed for both the oven and the analyser, and the measurement depends on accurate temperature readings and a known sample mass. The PRIME-1 experience shows that propulsion exhaust can appear in a mass spectrometer's data, so exhaust separation and background measurements are operational requirements [6]. Operations in permanently shadowed regions also depend on illumination and power planning, as the Athena landing outcome showed [6]. The VAPoR design shows some engineering responses, including a calcium oxide scrubber for CO2 and CO, getters regenerated by heating to 900 °C, and a gas handling system that needs no pumps or carrier gases [4].
article.limitations: Sample integrity is a major limit. The LUWA abstract identifies sublimation losses, adsorption effects and isotopic fractionation during sample handling as challenges [2]. Apollo samples may have lost volatiles before analysis [1]. A drilled or scooped sample may also be heated, exposed to exhaust or subjected to sublimation before it reaches the oven. Quantification depends on calibration against known standards, and the LightWAVE paper does not give its calibration constants [1]. Ground-test detection limits do not guarantee the same performance in the field [2]. As a general engineering point, the temperature at which a gas appears depends on heating rate, pressure and sample geometry, so release temperatures from different instruments are not directly comparable unless those conditions are reported.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A thermal volatile analyser would be a surface or mobile payload, or part of a sample chain on a lander or rover. Integration would include installation in a lander or rover on Earth with contamination control, launch and lunar transfer, landing and deployment, and connection of power, data and thermal interfaces. For drilling or mobile systems, it would also include sample acquisition and transfer into the oven [2][4].
transportation_process: Integrate the analyser into a lander or rover on Earth with contamination control and thermal protection for the sample chain.
Launch and transfer towards the Moon.
Land or deliver the payload to the surface; for probe-based designs such as LUWA, deployment is by a probe rather than a fixed lander.
Connect power, data and thermal interfaces.
For drilling or mobile systems, acquire the sample and transfer it into the oven without loss or contamination.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The VAPoR concept assumes that regolith samples are delivered to its inlet by a lander or rover scoop or drill, or collected and delivered by an astronaut [4]. The LUWA design places its analysers on a probe, which the source calls a mini-flying probe [2] and Wikipedia calls a mini-hopping probe [5]. The PRIME-1 system was integrated on the IM-2 lander [6].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The IM-2 Athena mission carried PRIME-1, whose lander came to rest on its side in a crater where sunlight could not reach its solar cells, illustrating how a landing orientation or illumination problem can end operations early [6]. TEGA was flown on the Phoenix Mars lander, not on a lunar mission [3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with a specific lander, rover or spacecraft has not been verified for any instrument in this article. The mass, dimensions, mounting points, power and data interfaces needed for such an assessment were not publicly specified in the consulted sources, so no compatibility claim is made.

article.historical_significance: TEGA demonstrated on Mars the combination of small heated ovens, a mass spectrometer and calorimetry for analysing soil and rock [3]. This gives the approach flight heritage, although the instrument was not designed for the Moon. VAPoR's selection for funding in 2007 [4] and the laboratory work on heated Apollo soils [4] established a lunar-directed pyrolysis approach. The LightWAVE methodology followed in 2022 [1], and the LUVMI sampler and analyser were developed as a prototype [7]. PRIME-1 on IM-2 was the first lunar flight in the sources consulted to carry a drill and a mass spectrometer for volatile analysis, although no volatile results were reported [6]. The LUWA mission's significance will depend on whether Chang'e-7 launches and returns in-situ data [2][5].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name "thermal volatile analyser" does not correspond to a single instrument in the sources consulted, so this article covers a class of related instruments. No source provided a validated mass, power or dimension for a lunar thermal volatile analyser. The VAPoR mass and power values are estimates from a concept paper [4]. The LUWA mass, power and dimensions are not stated [2]. The LUWA values come from a summarised fetch of the EGU26 abstract, not a verbatim copy, and should be checked against the original abstract before reuse [2]. The Chang'e-7 launch date is uncertain: the abstract gives 2026 [2], while the Wikipedia article gives a planned 2027 [5]. The link between LUWA and the Water Molecule and Hydrogen Isotope Analyzer listed in the Wikipedia article was not confirmed [5]. For PRIME-1, the NASA primary page was not read directly. The description relies on a Space Policy Online article that reports NASA statements [6]. MSolo's mass range and detailed results are unverified. For the Lunar Volatiles Scout, the derivation of its analyser from an earlier flown instrument, and the mass figures given in other sources, were not confirmed against the TUM page, so those values are not used [7]. The launch date and operating dates of the Phoenix mission were not verified in this run. The ten Kate et al. VAPoR paper was not read in full. ESA's PROSPECT concept, which uses a sealed oven, was identified only in search summaries and is not described here. No verified direct image asset was retrieved for any example, so the article contains no images. These gaps mean the article gives a source-limited overview rather than a complete technical audit.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image URLs were verified in this run, so no image objects are included.

data_quality_notes: The catalogue name 'Thermal volatile analyser' is a class name. The article covers related instruments and concepts and does not describe a single verified lunar instrument.
LUWA ground-test values come from a summarised fetch of the EGU26-2125 abstract and should be checked against the original abstract text.

Chang'e-7 launch date conflicts between sources: the abstract gives 2026; the Wikipedia article (last edited 29 October 2026) gives a planned 2027 after an indefinite delay. The Wikipedia article calls the probe a mini-hopping probe while the abstract calls it a mini-flying probe.
The link between LUWA and the Water Molecule and Hydrogen Isotope Analyzer listed in Wikipedia was not confirmed.
VAPoR mass, power, volume and telemetry values are estimates from a concept paper, not measurements. The breadboard temperature (1200 C) is a laboratory test on a simulant.
Lunar Volatiles Scout analyser ion-trap derivation and sampler heating temperature were not verified on the TUM page; conflicting rover mass figures from other sources were not used.
PRIME-1 details rely on Space Policy Online reporting NASA statements; the NASA primary page and MSolo mass range were not verified. No volatile measurement result was reported.
Phoenix launch date and operating dates were not verified in this run.
The ten Kate et al. 2010 VAPoR paper was not read in full. ESA PROSPECT was identified only in search summaries and is not described.
